choices.A: The limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing developed by Lang provides a means of explaining the finding by van Berlo et al. that players may not readily recollect the brand and product information embedded in advergames.
choices.B: Research by van Berlo et al. corroborates Lang’s conclusion that because people predominantly focus on game mechanics when playing video games, it is difficult for advergames to communicate brand and product information in ways that are highly memorable.
choices.C: The meta-analysis by van Berlo et al. reveals that higher engagement in advergame mechanics is linked to lower effectiveness in persuading players to purchase particular brands and products.
choices.D: Although the limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing developed by Lang suggests otherwise, advergames can succeed as marketing tools, provided that they achieve a balance between game mechanics and the promotion of a brand or product.

rationale: Choice A is the best answer because it most accurately states the main idea of the text. The text begins by presenting van Berlo et al.’s finding that advergames—video games intended to promote a specific product or service—can be engaging to players but “may not facilitate subsequent recall of product and brand information,” ultimately limiting their effectiveness as advertisements. The text then suggests that Lang’s limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing, which characterizes cognitive capacity as finite, can explain or account for van Berlo et al.’s finding: specifically, players’ attention is “directed foremost toward the advergame’s mechanics” instead of toward the advertising information. The main idea of the text is therefore that Lang’s model provides a means of explaining van Berlo et al.’s finding.

Choice B is incorrect because it mischaracterizes the relationship between Lang’s model and van Berlo et al.’s finding. The text presents Lang’s model as a broad theoretical framework about cognitive capacity that can explain van Berlo et al.’s finding. The text doesn’t indicate that Lang drew conclusions specific to video games that van Berlo et al. then corroborated. Choice C is incorrect because it mischaracterizes the findings of the meta-analysis by van Berlo et al. Although Lang’s model suggests that engagement in advergame mechanics occurs at the expense of recalling advertising information, the text doesn’t indicate that van Berlo et al. offered this explanation for their finding. The text merely states that van Berlo et al. found that advergames “can elicit player interest” but “may not facilitate subsequent recall of product and brand information.” In addition, the text doesn’t discuss whether players’ ability to recall advertising content ultimately affects their purchasing behavior. Choice D is incorrect. Although the text presents Lang’s model as an explanation of why advergames may not succeed in promoting recall of advertising information, the text doesn’t suggest that advergames can succeed as marketing tools if they balance mechanics and promotion. The text doesn’t propose a design solution to the limitations of advergames or suggest that these limitations can be overcome.
stem: In their meta-analysis of research on advergames (video games developed to promote products or services), Zeph M.C. van Berlo et al. confirm that such games, though they can elicit player interest, may not facilitate subsequent recall of product and brand information. This phenomenon can be explained by the finite nature of cognitive capacity as it is articulated in Annie Lang’s limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing. In this case, players’ cognitive resources are directed foremost toward the advergame’s mechanics, leaving little or no capacity for encoding and storing the information the advertiser intends to be salient.
